note: Teaching examples written for this project, with the reason each form is correct.
why: The topics' own examples come from the source documents: they show a form in use and stop there. A learner reading “den alten Mann” is shown the ending and left to work out where it came from, which is the step they cannot take yet — it is the thing being taught. These carry that reason. They are kept apart from the source examples rather than mixed into them, because the source carries an attribution and these are ours. None of them reuses the answer to one of the topic's practice exercises.

sentences.why: ich always takes -e. The stem is wohn-, so the form is wohne.
du takes -st, in a question exactly as in a statement — only the word order moves.
The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so an extra -e goes in before the ending: arbeitet, not arbeitt.
wir takes -en, which is also the form the dictionary lists.

contrast.why: A stem ending in -t or -d cannot take -st directly — you could not say it. The -e is there to make the ending pronounceable.

sentences.why: Nominative masculine: the dog is doing the sleeping, so the ending is -e.
Accusative masculine: now the dog is what is seen. This is the only accusative box that changes to -en.

sentences.de: Ich spiele mit dem kleinen Hund.
sentences.en: I am playing with the little dog.
sentences.why: mit always takes the dative, and every dative box is -en — gender makes no difference here.
Plural: -en in every case, so the plural never has to be worked out.

contrast.why: The article already changed to den, so the adjective has to change too. Masculine is the one gender where the accusative differs from the nominative — in neuter and feminine the -e really would be right.

sentences.why: Der Lehrer does the explaining (nominative); die Aufgabe is what is explained (accusative). Feminine looks the same in both, so only the masculine shows the change.
danken takes the dative — the thanks go to someone. Masculine der becomes dem.

sentences.en: The book belongs to the children.
sentences.why: gehören takes the dative, and this is the plural — so the article is den and the noun itself adds -n.

contrast.why: den is the accusative. danken never takes an accusative object, so the ending has to be the dative dem — a small group of verbs (danken, helfen, gehören, gefallen) work this way and are worth learning together.

sentences.de: Ich bleibe heute zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
sentences.en: I am staying at home today because I am ill.
sentences.why: weil sends the conjugated verb to the very end: bin is the last word, not after ich.

sentences.de: Sie lernt Deutsch, weil sie in Wien studieren will.
sentences.en: She is learning German because she wants to study in Vienna.
sentences.why: With a modal verb the conjugated one still goes last, so the order ends studieren will — the infinitive comes before it.

sentences.de: Ich glaube, dass er morgen kommt.
sentences.en: I think that he is coming tomorrow.
sentences.why: dass works exactly like weil for word order. The difference is meaning: dass reports what you think, weil gives a reason.

sentences.de: Weil es regnet, nehme ich den Bus.
sentences.en: Because it is raining, I am taking the bus.
sentences.why: The weil-clause can come first. Then it fills the first position, so the main clause starts with its verb: nehme ich, not ich nehme.

contrast.wrong: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin krank.
contrast.right: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
contrast.why: This is the commonest mistake with weil, because English keeps the verb in place. In German weil moves it to the end — denn is the connector that leaves it alone.

sentences.de: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
sentences.en: I am hanging the picture on the wall.
sentences.why: The picture moves to a new place, so this answers wohin? and the article is accusative: die Wand.

sentences.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
sentences.en: The picture is hanging on the wall.
sentences.why: Nothing moves — it is already there. That answers wo?, so the article is dative: der Wand.

sentences.de: Die Katze springt auf den Tisch.
sentences.en: The cat jumps onto the table.
sentences.why: Jumping onto is movement to a new place: accusative den.

sentences.de: Die Katze schläft auf dem Tisch.
sentences.en: The cat is sleeping on the table.
sentences.why: Sleeping is not going anywhere: dative dem.

contrast.why: Ich gehe in der Stadt is not wrong German, but it means walking around inside the town. For going into town you need the accusative: in die Stadt. The case is what carries the difference.

sentences.why: Active: the subject is the one doing it.
Passive: what was the object is now the subject, and the doer has disappeared because it does not matter who repairs it.

sentences.de: Der Computer wird von dem Techniker repariert.
sentences.en: The computer is being repaired by the technician.
sentences.why: When the doer does matter, von plus the dative brings it back.
Only werden changes for plural. The participle stays exactly as it was.

contrast.wrong: Der Computer ist repariert worden von dem Techniker.
contrast.right: Der Computer ist von dem Techniker repariert worden.
contrast.why: German does not leave the von-phrase after the verb at the end. The participle closes the sentence, so everything else comes before it.

sentences.de: Der Kurs war teuer. Dafür war er sehr gut.
sentences.en: The course was expensive. In return it was very good.
sentences.why: dafür balances: the cost stays true, and this makes up for it.

sentences.de: Der Kurs war teuer. Stattdessen lernte ich allein.
sentences.en: The course was expensive. Instead I studied on my own.
sentences.why: stattdessen replaces: the course did not happen, this did. Swapping it for dafür would change the facts, not just the wording.

sentences.de: Ich kenne die Stadt gut. Da habe ich studiert.
sentences.en: I know the city well. That is where I studied.
sentences.why: da points back at a place already named, so the sentence does not have to repeat it.

sentences.de: Er kam zu spät. Dadurch verpassten wir den Zug.
sentences.en: He arrived late. That made us miss the train.
sentences.why: dadurch names the cause: the lateness is what produced the result.

contrast.wrong: Das Hotel war laut. Dafür haben wir ein anderes genommen.
contrast.right: Das Hotel war laut. Stattdessen haben wir ein anderes genommen.
contrast.why: dafür would mean the noise was compensated for somehow. Here the hotel was swapped, which is a replacement — stattdessen.

sentences.why: haben is the part that gets conjugated, and it stands second. The participle never changes and waits at the end of the sentence.
The participle is the same word as before. Only haben moved — habe for ich, haben for wir — which is why it is the only part you have to think about.
ankommen is a movement to a new place, so the auxiliary is sein and not haben.
A change of state counts as movement for this rule: asleep to awake, so sein again.

contrast.why: Movement to a new place takes sein. Reaching for haben here is the commonest mistake in the perfect, because English has only one auxiliary.

sentences.why: fahren turns its a into ä, but only for du and er / sie / es. The -st on the end is the ordinary du ending and is not part of the change.
sprechen turns e into i for er / sie / es. Note there is no -t ending visible beyond the stem's own: spricht, not sprichtt.
wir keeps the infinitive untouched — the e is back. This is the same verb as the sentence above, which is the point.
ihr does not change the vowel either, even though du liest and er liest both do. Only two persons in the whole paradigm change.

contrast.why: The ending was right; the stem vowel was not. du is one of the two persons that have to change it.

sentences.why: The modal is what gets conjugated, and it takes the second position. The verb carrying the meaning goes right to the end, as a plain infinitive.
In a question the modal moves to the front. The infinitive does not follow it — it still waits at the end.

sentences.en: We wanted to go to the cinema.
sentences.why: A modal in the past uses the preterite, wollten. Only the modal changes; gehen is exactly as it was.

sentences.en: He is not allowed to smoke here.
sentences.why: ich and er take no ending on a modal: darf, never darft. Everything else in the sentence, nicht included, sits between the two verbs.

contrast.why: A modal takes a bare infinitive. The zu belongs with verbs like versuchen and hoffen, never with a modal.

sentences.en: I was looking for my key.
sentences.why: The regular preterite is the stem plus -te. Nothing else is added for ich.

sentences.en: He was looking for it too.
sentences.why: Identical to the ich form. The preterite is the one tense that does not tell ich and er apart, so the subject has to.
The stem ends in -t, so an -e- goes in before the ending: warteten. Without it the word would be unsayable.
Irregular: the stem itself changed, from geh- to ging-, and then ich and er take no ending at all.

contrast.why: An irregular verb changes its stem instead of adding -te. Doing both at once is the mistake.

sentences.why: ihn is the accusative of er. He is what is being seen, so he is the object, and the object form is a different word.
Swap who is doing the seeing and both pronouns change shape: er becomes the subject, ich becomes mich.
helfen takes a dative object, so it is ihm, not ihn. The verb decides the case — the meaning gives no clue.
Two objects at once. The thing handed over is accusative, and the person who receives it is dative: mir.

contrast.why: helfen is one of the verbs that demand a dative object. Nothing in the English hints at it, so it has to be learned together with the verb.

sentences.why: ein gives nothing away about the gender, so the adjective has to carry it: -er says masculine.
The same ein, a different ending. -es says neuter. The adjective is doing the work the article cannot do here.
Now einen itself shows masculine accusative, so the adjective no longer has to — it falls back to the weak -en.
mein- declines exactly like ein-, so there is nothing new to learn: feminine gives -e.

contrast.why: Hund is masculine, so the ending has to be -er. With -es the sentence claims Hund is neuter.

sentences.de: Als ich klein war, wohnte ich in Berlin.
sentences.en: When I was small, I lived in Berlin.
sentences.why: One stretch of the past, looked back on once: als. Its own verb goes last, and because the als clause takes position 1 the main clause has to begin with its verb.

sentences.de: Immer wenn es regnete, blieben wir zu Hause.
sentences.en: Whenever it rained, we stayed at home.
sentences.why: Also in the past, but repeated, so wenn and not als. Immer is what makes the repetition explicit.

sentences.de: Wenn ich Zeit habe, rufe ich dich an.
sentences.en: When I have time, I will call you.
sentences.why: Present or future is always wenn, once or many times — the als / wenn choice only exists in the past.

sentences.de: Ich war glücklich, als ich das hörte.
sentences.en: I was happy when I heard that.
sentences.why: The main clause can come first. Then it keeps its ordinary order and only the als clause sends its verb to the end.

contrast.wrong: Wenn ich klein war, wohnte ich in Berlin.
contrast.right: Als ich klein war, wohnte ich in Berlin.
contrast.why: Both are well-formed German, but they say different things: wenn would mean it happened again and again. For one continuous stretch of the past, German needs als.

sentences.de: Das ist der Mann, der hier wohnt.
sentences.en: That is the man who lives here.
sentences.why: Mann is masculine, so the pronoun is masculine. He is the subject of his own clause, so it is nominative — der. The verb goes last.

sentences.de: Das ist der Mann, den ich kenne.
sentences.en: That is the man I know.
sentences.why: Still masculine, because Mann has not changed. But now he is what I know, so the case does change: accusative den.

sentences.de: Das ist die Frau, der ich geholfen habe.
sentences.en: That is the woman I helped.
sentences.why: The gender comes from Frau and the case from the verb inside the clause. helfen takes the dative, and dative feminine is der.

sentences.de: Das sind die Leute, denen ich geholfen habe.
sentences.en: Those are the people I helped.
sentences.why: Dative plural is the single form that is not the same as the definite article: denen, not den.

contrast.wrong: Das ist die Frau, die ich geholfen habe.
contrast.right: Das ist die Frau, der ich geholfen habe.
contrast.why: die would be right if she were the direct object, but geholfen demands a dative, and the dative feminine is der.

sentences.why: haben takes an accusative object, and masculine accusative is the one singular box where ein- has to show an ending.
Feminine accusative is identical to the nominative — eine. Three of the four boxes do not change at all, which is why the masculine one is worth remembering.

sentences.de: Ich gebe meinem Bruder das Buch.
sentences.en: I give my brother the book.
sentences.why: Dative masculine takes -em. mein- carries exactly the endings ein- does, so there is only one set to learn.
kein- is ein- with a k in front of it, and in the plural it takes -e — the same ending the definite article shows.

contrast.why: The object of haben is accusative, and masculine accusative is precisely the box where ein- must not stay bare.
